title: Expanding approaches to teaching for diversity and justice in K-12 education: Fostering global citizenship across the content areas
extended_summary:
This paper asks what globally competent teaching looks like in K-12 classrooms across multiple subject areas and grade levels, and what recurring pedagogical patterns might define that work. The authors note that while global citizenship and global competence are increasingly emphasized in standards, there has been limited empirical research on how in-service teachers actually enact these ideas outside of social studies and foreign language classrooms.

To address this gap, the study conducts a qualitative multiple case analysis of 10 in-service teachers in North Carolina who were already committed to teaching for global competence. The teachers worked across elementary, middle, and high school settings and taught English language arts, science, math, music, social studies, world languages, and all-subject elementary classes. Data included biographical interviews, classroom observations, post-observation interviews, focus groups, and teaching artifacts such as lesson plans and rubrics. The analysis used a priori codes drawn from global competence literature and then inductively identified surface, deep, and implicit structures of teaching.

The paper concludes that three signature pedagogies characterize globally competent teaching across content areas: intentional integration of global topics and multiple perspectives into the standard curriculum; ongoing authentic engagement with global issues through tasks like pen pals, Skype exchanges, service learning, and letters to public officials; and connecting teachers’ own global experiences with students’ experiences and curriculum. Across cases, these practices were linked to an implicit goal of fostering empathy, layered/global citizenship identities, and responsible action. The authors argue that these recurring practices can inform policy, teacher preparation, and professional development for global citizenship education in K-12 schools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative multiple-case study, which provides credible descriptive evidence but no causal estimation. The paper is methodologically clear, but it does not evaluate an AI/technology intervention or report quantitative outcome effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The study has conceptual and policy relevance for K-12 global citizenship teaching, but it does not measure student outcome gains from an intervention. Its impact is therefore indirect and primarily illustrative rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.
